source_text: At nunc, postquam pro medicamine coepit offerri, et delectationi accessit auctoritas, ut consensu pene mundi, membripotens regina mentium, expugnatrix honestatis, et invicta animorum omnium captivatrix turpitudo baccharetur; nobis quanto honestior, tanto durior tuendae veritatis causa facta est. Quia contra praecipites populos et suis remediis infensos, non multum valet raritas oratione medicantium. Quid igitur? Horumne intuitu, receptui canere debebimus, et contumelias nostras ultum ire silentio, ac de conscientiae portu aliorum ridere naufragia? Verum contradicit huic odio, primo benignitas quam generi debemus humano; deinceps spes et fides, quam habemus in Deum, qui extra id quod frequenter desperatas temporum levavit ruinas; constantiam tamen quam usque ad mortis horam exerceri voluit, etiamsi nullus in praesentiarum sequeretur effectus, aeterna remuneratione donavit.
pass_a_gloss: But now, after it has begun to be offered in place of medicine, and authority has been added to delight, so that, with the consent of almost the world, shamefulness, queen of minds powerful through the members, stormer of decency, and undefeated capturer of all souls, may revel; for us the cause of guarding the truth has been made as much harder as it is more honorable. Because against headlong peoples and those hostile to their own remedies the rarity of those healing by speech does not avail much. What then? At the sight of these, shall we sound the retreat, and avenge our insults by silence, and from the harbor of conscience laugh at others' shipwrecks? But first the kindness which we owe to the human race contradicts this hatred; next the hope and faith which we have in God, who besides this, that he has frequently lifted the desperate ruins of times, has nevertheless gifted with eternal recompense the constancy which he wanted to be exercised even to the hour of death, even if no effect followed in the present.

lemmas.lexica: LS ratio; Blaise use of reason required for sin

pass_b_english: But now it has begun to be offered as medicine, and pleasure has gained the support of authority. With almost the whole world’s consent, shamelessness runs riot: the queen of minds, ruling through the bodily organs, the conqueror of decency, the undefeated captor of every soul. The more honorable our defense of truth, the harder it has therefore become. For the few who heal through speech have little power against reckless crowds hostile to their own remedies. What then? Should we sound the retreat at the sight of them, avenge the insults we have suffered by keeping silent, and laugh at others’ shipwrecks from the safe harbor of our conscience? But first, the goodwill we owe the human race opposes such hatred. So do our hope and faith in God. Besides repeatedly restoring the seemingly hopeless wreckage of the times, God has rewarded with eternal recompense the steadfastness he wished us to exercise until death, even when no result followed in the present.

choices.why: For Julian, sin requires rational choice; infants lack usus rationis.
Julian: Paul says death passed to all, not sin; distinguish temporal death from eternal punishment.

anf_compare.notes: Victorian English of some of Julian survives inside NPNF Augustine (chiefly On Marriage and Concupiscence and related anti-Pelagian books). NPNF was not copied. Pass A is a literal gloss of Augustinus.it Latin of Julian's words only; Augustine's replies in the same locus are excluded.

speaker: Julian of Eclanum (words preserved in Augustine, Opus imperfectum contra Iulianum); Augustine's reply at this locus is excluded.
